id_and_class.summary: Kevin J. Mitchell proposes that a theory of consciousness should be judged by whether it can address fifteen linked questions, from which things are conscious, through content, unity, selfhood, and qualia, to how conscious states control behavior. A framework that related all fifteen coherently, even without answering them, would in his view count as a theory of consciousness.
id_and_class.core_identity_tagline: Fifteen Questions a Theory of Consciousness Must Answer

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Mitchell offers no identity claim. He defines the explanatory target of a theory of consciousness as the set of fifteen questions and the relations among them.
conceptual_ground.mind_body_relationship: The questions presuppose that consciousness depends on neural activity, asking why some neural activity feels like something and how the meaning of mental states can constrain neural circuits.
conceptual_ground.emergence_type: Left open; the Mentality Question asks when computation becomes cognition and cognition becomes cogitation
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: Posed as open problems: why experiences feel like ours (Selfhood), and how conscious states come to be about things when the states are all the system can access (Intentionality).
conceptual_ground.qualia_account: Posed as an open problem: why some neural activity feels like anything, why different signals feel different, and why each feels the specific way it does.
conceptual_ground.constituents_and_structure: Fifteen questions grouped into related domains: Which, Awareness, Capacity, State, Content, Attention, Architecture, Unity, Selfhood, Qualia, Valence, Intentionality, Function, Mentality, and Control.

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Phenomenal, access, attention, self-awareness, unity, valence, intentionality, function, agency, and free will.
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: Explanatory completeness as the test of a theory: a theory must provide a coherent framework that relates all fifteen questions to one another.
mechanism_and_dynamics.location_and_distribution: Posed as the Architecture Question: which systems support conscious perception, and whether information is pushed into a common space or a central system points to distributed representations.
mechanism_and_dynamics.causation_and_functional_role: Posed as the Function and Control Questions: what adaptive value conscious experience and metacognition have, and how conscious activity influences behavior.
mechanism_and_dynamics.integration_or_binding: Posed as the Unity Question: why consciousness feels unitary and how separate informational streams are bound together.
mechanism_and_dynamics.information_flow_or_representation: Posed as the Content Question: why some information reaches conscious awareness while most is excluded.
core_claims_and_evidence: A theory of consciousness must say which kinds of things are conscious and what separates them from things that are not.
It must distinguish the capacity for consciousness from the state of being conscious, and both from the contents of consciousness.
It must explain how homeostatic control signals with valence relate to subjective feeling.
Relating all fifteen questions in one coherent framework, even without answering them, would amount to a theory of consciousness.
mechanism_and_dynamics.basis_of_belief_or_evidence_type: Conceptual: a neuroscientist’s analysis of what an explanation of consciousness must cover.

empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: By design the framework answers none of its questions; it sets the standard other theories must meet.
